catalog_quote: 4. SUPRASEGMENTALS. Stress in Irarutu language is phonemic. The stress is identified by high pitch when the stressed syllable is not followed by the syllable with a schwa. Vowel length does not occur on the stressed syllable. /debé/ [dəbé] 'pukul' 'to hit'; /tepú/ [təpú] 'di bawah' 'under'; /pití/ ... 'a kind of mouse'; /waráda/ [wařáda] 'pisau' 'knife'; /wararú/ [wařařú] 'berita' 'news'. [p.48] The vowel length occurs in the stressed syllable when the stressed syllable is followed by the syllable with a schwa. In such cases, a gliding pitch also occurs on the stressed syllable. /dábe/ [dá:bə] 'menumbuk, memukul' 'to pound'; /tápe/ [tá:pə] 'menikam' 'to stab'; /píte/ [pí:tə] 'jahat' 'evil'; /rádeni/ [řá:dənɩ] 'pakaian' 'clothing'; /dedáne/ [dədá:nə] 'kebun' 'garden'. ... [endnote 2, p.55] There have been other alternatives for the schwa analysis. Other options for an analysis of schwa a…

new_statements.quote: p.110: "Stress is phonemic as shown by: ɔrɔ'e nggáta 'who are you?' - ərə' nga tá 'you eat shit'. In words with more than one vowel phoneme however the stress usually is on the last vowel phoneme: e.g. fan 'pig'." p.111: "In polysyllabic words stress will be marked when it is carried by another vowel than the last one. The stress marker is '. Thus, the example of 'you shot the pig' given above will be written ɔmasəmbenggat fanɛ." p.110 (word-final release): "Although this vowel is non-phonemic because it is predictable, it can serve as the carrier of stress when a word is uttered in isolation and with extra emphasis, e.g. in an eliciting situation. Thus I recorded: ['no:ndə no'ndə] 'he holds it'."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: 66-page image-only scan of IRIAN vol. XVII, two journal pages per PDF page). Re-rendered PDF pp.57-58 myself at 200 dpi and read the page images directly (scanned file consulted only for locating passages). p.110 (PDF p.58 left, last paragraph of the Phonology section) reads exactly: 'Stress is phonemic as shown by: ɔrɔ'e nggáta 'who are you?' - ərə' nga tá 'you eat shit'. In words with more than one vowel phoneme however the stress usually is on the last vowel phoneme: e.g. fan 'pig'.' The printed 'fan' is followed by a visible gap before 'pig', consistent with the reader's note that a character (final ɛ) dropped in typesetting; the same word is printed fanɛ / [əfa'nɛ] four paragraphs earl…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Irarutu (catalog-all-2026-09-12) with an EMPTY rule and there are no existing stress statements, so this source supplies the placement: default final stress ('usually on the last vowel phoneme') with stress called phonemic and non-final stress treated as the marked case. Nothing to contradict. Describes the Fruata dialect only (p.109).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls by default on the last vowel phoneme of a polysyllabic word (final syllable); Voorhoeve nonetheless calls stress phonemic on the strength of one contrasting pair (ɔrɔ'e nggáta 'who are you?' vs ərə' nga tá 'you eat shit'), and his orthography marks stress only when it is not on the last vowel, i.e. non-final stress is the marked exception. The example 'pig' is printed as 'fan' (a character may have dropped in typesetting; the same word appears on pp.110-111 as [əfa'nɛ] / fanɛ with final stress).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Stress is called phonemic; one minimal-pair-style contrast is given (ɔrɔ'e nggáta vs ərə' nga tá), so some words/phrases carry non-final stress, which the spelling marks with an apostrophe. (2) The predictable non-phonemic word-final vocalic release [ə] can carry stress when a word is said in isolation with extra emphasis: ['no:ndə no'ndə] 'he holds it'. (3) In pretonic position a vowel phoneme can reduce to a mid-central [ə̌] (p.110). (4) No statement on secondary stress; monosyllables not discussed beyond 'more than one vowel phoneme'.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve 1989 states explicitly (p.109): "The bulk of my data is in the Fruata dialect as this was the dialect spoken by my main informants. The following notes therefore describe only the Fruata variant of Irarutu." He lists seven local dialects (Nabi, Babo, Kasuri, Fruata, South-Arguni, East-Arguni, North-Arguni) and notes (p.108) that speakers distinguish them partly by "rimla, a local term covering intonation, stress patterns, and speed of speech" — so stress patterns may differ across dialects; the final-stress statement is for Fruata.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim on printed p.47 (PDF p.18) of the Matsumura 1991 PDF we hold, page image inspected; p.48 and endnote 2 p.55 match the scanned layer. (2) Deciding source is a 1991 SIL/UNCEN phonology working paper; the best available description, Jackson 2014 (451-pp reference grammar with a dedicated 'Stress and accent' section and a spectrogram), is already held by the project under our earlier reading and independently states 'Stress in Irarutu is not predictable.. lexically determined.. Irarutu has phonemic stress', with final and penultimate stress about equally frequent and minimal pair [fi.'na] vs ['fi.na]. So lexical is confirmed by the strongest source; nothing suggests a reclassify. (3) Voorhoeve 1989 downloaded now (IRIAN 17, the Internet Archive of papuaweb): 'Stress is phonemic.. however the stress usually is on the last vowel phoneme' — this is the primary basis of StressTyp2 U
